title: Decoding the Aneurysm Thrombus: Radiomic Signatures of Sac Shrinkage after Endovascular Aortic Repair.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Aneurysm sac shrinkage after endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) is a surrogate marker of effective aneurysm exclusion and favorable outcomes. Radiomics enables quantitative imaging analysis beyond visual assessment and is increasingly applied in cardiovascular imaging. Analysis of intraluminal thrombus (ILT) may provide additional information for identifying patients with different patterns of sac remodeling after EVAR. METHODS: This single-center retrospective study assessed whether radiomic features of the ILT extracted from preoperative computed tomography angiography (CTA), alone and in combination with clinical and anatomical variables, were associated with aneurysm sac shrinkage after EVAR. Patients undergoing elective EVAR for infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) were included and stratified according to sac shrinkage at a 12-month follow up. Preoperative arterial-phase CTA scans were analyzed. The aneurysm sac was manually segmented using three-dimensional (3D) slicer, and the ILT was selected as the region of interest. A total of 530 radiomic features were extracted using PyRadiomics with Laplacian of Gaussian filtering. Features were standardized and evaluated using the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test, Pearson's correlation filtering, and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)-based feature selection. Predictive performance was compared among combined clinical-radiomic, radiomic-only, and clinical-only models. RESULTS: Among 94 patients, 29 showed aneurysm sac shrinkage. Two radiomic features were significantly associated with shrinkage. Younger age (P = 0.02), larger aneurysm diameter (P = 0.02), and homogeneous thrombus texture were associated with shrinkage, while the absence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) was associated with lack of shrinkage. None of the other evaluated clinical or anatomical variables showed a significant association with sac shrinkage. The combined clinical-radiomic model achieved the best performance (area under the curve [AUC] 0.76, sensitivity 0.70, specificity 0.75, and accuracy 0.73). CONCLUSION: Preoperative thrombus radiomic features were associated with subsequent sac shrinkage and provided complementary information when integrated with clinical variables. These findings support the potential role of thrombus radiomics in the characterization of sac remodeling after EVAR and warrant validation in larger cohorts.

Radiomics enables quantitative imaging analysis beyond visual assessment and is increasingly applied in cardiovascular imaging. Analysis of intraluminal thrombus (ILT) may provide additional information for identifying patients with different patterns of sac remodeling after EVAR.

title: Use of smart glasses for ultrasound-guided central venous catheterization in adults: a randomized clinical trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Head-mounted displays can be integrated with ultrasonography to overlay the image in the operator's field of view, improving hand-eye coordination during invasive procedures. The clinical efficacy of smart glasses for central venous catheterization (CVC) remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate whether using smart glasses can improve efficiency compared to conventional ultrasound-guided CVC. METHODS: This prospective, single-blinded, controlled study enrolled adult patients who underwent elective surgery requiring CVC. Patients were assigned to either the ultrasound screen (control) or smart glasses group using stratified randomization according to operator qualification. The primary outcome was the overall CVC procedural time. Secondary outcomes included ultrasound scanning and venous access time, number of needle redirections and probe repositionings, procedural success and complication rates. RESULTS: In total, 124 patients were analyzed. The overall procedural time was significantly reduced in the smart glasses group compared to that in the control group (158 [140, 189] s vs. 134 [117,150] s; median difference, 26.0 s; 95% CI, [16.0-37.0] s, P < 0.001). Specifically, the ultrasound scanning time (median difference, 3.0 s, P = 0.004), venous access time (median difference, 2.0 s, P = 0.013), number of needle redirections (median difference, 1.0, P = 0.003) and probe repositionings (median difference, 0.0, P = 0.005) were significantly reduced in the smart glasses group compared to those in the control group. However, the success and complication rates were comparable between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Smart glasses modestly improved procedural efficiency in ultrasound-guided CVC, potientially for novices, without improving success or complication rates. Larger-sample studies with more diverse operators and patients are warranted. title: Endovascular Management With a Fenestration Technique of an Iatrogenic Thoracic Chronic Type B Aortic Dissection.
abstract: We report the case of an 86-year-old woman who developed an intraoperative type B aortic dissection during ascending aortic replacement for an ascending aortic aneurysm. Postoperative imaging demonstrated an uncomplicated dissection extending to the infrarenal aorta. At 10 weeks, follow-up imaging revealed rapid aneurysmal expansion of the false lumen. Thoracic endovascular aortic repair was performed with adjunctive cerebrospinal fluid drainage, rapid pacing, and image fusion guidance. An intimal fenestration technique was used to optimize the distal sealing zone, extending the disruption from a pre-existing re-entry tear. A type Ib endoleak necessitated additional stent-graft deployment, which in turn caused occlusion of the left renal and superior mesenteric arteries. The STABILISE technique (stent-assisted balloon-induced intimal disruption and relamination in aortic dissection repair) with a PETTICOAT (Provisional Extension To Induce Complete Attachment) bare stent restored renal perfusion, and targeted stenting re-established mesenteric flow. A postprocedural pseudoaneurysm was managed conservatively and resolved with spontaneous thrombosis within 48 hours. The patient was discharged on postoperative day seven, asymptomatic, with complete exclusion of the dissection, patent visceral vessels, and no endoleak confirmed at six-week follow-up. This case illustrates that combining distal flap fenestration with STABILISE relamination and a comprehensive endovascular toolkit can successfully manage complex chronic type B aortic dissections, even in elderly, high-risk patients-provided that adequate perioperative safety measures and a broad endovascular armamentarium are available to address unanticipated complications.

Postoperative imaging demonstrated an uncomplicated dissection extending to the infrarenal aorta. At 10 weeks, follow-up imaging revealed rapid aneurysmal expansion of the false lumen.

title: Atheroembolic Blue Toe Syndrome Progressing to Below-Knee Amputation Despite Attempted Source Control and Revascularization: A Case Report.
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa Staphylococcus aureus Blue toe syndrome is characterized by painful blue or violaceous discoloration of one or more toes caused by impaired digital arterial perfusion. We present a 72-year-old woman with peripheral arterial disease, diabetes mellitus, antiphospholipid syndrome, and prior thromboembolic disease who developed dusky-blue discoloration of the left third toe. Initial arterial duplex demonstrated no major arterial occlusion, while computed tomography angiography with runoff showed distal infrarenal aortic soft plaque and distal tibial/pedal arterial disease. The aortic lesion was considered the suspected proximal embolic source in the setting of concomitant distal tibial and pedal arterial disease. The patient underwent endovascular aortic repair for proximal source control, but the left third toe nevertheless progressed to dry gangrene and required amputation. Over the following months, she developed nonhealing wounds, infections withand methicillin-resistant(MRSA), worsened distal perfusion, and osteomyelitis. There were multiple limb salvage procedures, including angioplasty, toe amputation, common plantar embolectomy, plantar bypass, transmetatarsal amputation, Achilles tendon lengthening, antibiotic bead placement, and external fixation. Following these procedures, however, the foot developed worsening ischemic and infected tissue loss and needed an emergency left below-knee amputation. Final pathology demonstrated significant findings, including gangrenous necrosis, chronic osteomyelitis, calcific atherosclerosis, and tibial vessel occlusions. This case showcases how blue toe syndrome can progress despite source control when severe distal runoff disease, poor wound oxygenation, and recurrent infections are present.

title: Sequential Arch-Tear Eligibility for Uncovered Aortic Arch Stent in Acute DeBakey Type I Aortic Dissection.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Because an uncovered arch scaffold does not provide a covered seal across an unresected arch tear, we evaluated a source-adjudicated sequential eligibility framework separating study-defined stop gates from residual-risk modifiers. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 266 patients with acute DeBakey type I dissection treated by hemiarch repair alone (No. = 160) or hemiarch plus AMDS (No. = 106). Blinded preoperative CT-scan re-review validated Gate 1 (visible arch tear), and operative-report review confirmed Gate 2 (tear directly observed at open inspection). Supra-aortic false-lumen communication was assessed only after both gates were negative. RESULTS: p p p Sixty-nine patients (25.9%) passed both study-defined gates (AMDS = 32; hemiarch = 37). Twelve-month CT-scan was available in 45/69 (65.2%; AMDS 24/32, hemiarch 21/37). Among imaged patients, complete zone 2-3 false-lumen exclusion occurred in 20/24 (83.3%) after AMDS and 0/21 after hemiarch (risk difference +83.3 percentage points, 95% CI +58.7 to +93.3;< 0.001). DANE occurred in 4/32 (12.5%) and 16/37 (43.2%), respectively (= 0.007). Under the adverse opposing missingness scenario, the exclusion risk difference narrowed to +19.3 percentage points (95% CI -4.2 to +39.9;= 0.148). CONCLUSIONS: These findings are hypothesis-generating and apply to a selected post hoc subgroup; treatment comparisons are non-causal. Prospective external validation of the study-defined hierarchy remains required.

title: Baricitinib Efficacy Through 4 Years in Responders and Safety up to 5 Years in Adults with Severe Alopecia Areata: Final Results from BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Long-term efficacy and safety data are imperative for therapies used to treat severe alopecia areata (AA) because the disease is chronic, loss of response can be devastating to patients, and the safety profile needs to support long-term therapy. Baricitinib, a selective JAK inhibitor, has been approved for severe AA in adults and is being studied in pediatric patients. This study evaluates the final long-term efficacy and safety of baricitinib in adults with severe AA. METHODS: Efficacy was assessed for patients randomized to baricitinib 4 mg or 2 mg who achieved response (Severity of Alopecia Tool [SALT] score ≤ 20) at Week 52 (4 mg, N = 133; 2 mg, N = 72) and stayed on the same dose through Week 200. Proportions of patients maintaining a SALT score ≤ 20 and achieving a Clinician-Reported Outcome Measure for Eyebrow/Eyelash (EB/EL) Hair Loss™ score of 0 or 1 with ≥ 2-point improvement from baseline were reported using the modified last-observation-carried-forward method. Safety is reported as incidence rates (IR) per 100 patient-years at risk for the All BARI AA group (N = 1303) and Extended BARI AA group (N = 948) through 248 weeks of exposure RESULTS: For baricitinib 4 mg and 2 mg, respectively, among Week 52 responders, 115/133 (86.5%) and 61/72 (84.7%) maintained a SALT score ≤ 20 at Week 200. Regrowth of EB/EL hair continued beyond Week 52 and was maintained through Week 200. In up to 5 years of exposure with baricitinib, the IR for serious infections, nonmelanoma skin cancer malignancies, deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism, and major adverse cardiovascular events remained low relative to background rates. No deaths occurred, and adverse event rates remained stable over time. CONCLUSIONS: Within this population, ~ 85% of responders maintained SALT scores ≤ 20 through approximately 4 years with continued benefit for EB/EL. Baricitinib's safety profile remained consistent over 5 years of treatment, in line with prior BRAVE program findings. title: Paget-Schroetter Syndrome With Focal Subclavian Arterial Stenosis Following Repetitive Overhead Activity: A Case Report.
abstract: Paget-Schroetter syndrome (PSS), also known as effort thrombosis, is a rare form of upper extremity deep vein thrombosis resulting from mechanical compression of the subclavian vein at the thoracic outlet. It typically occurs in young, active individuals performing strenuous upper limb exercises and presents with pain, swelling, and discoloration of the affected limb. Early diagnosis and specialist management are important for optimizing outcomes. In selected patients, management may include a combined endovascular and surgical approach to restore venous patency and reduce the risk of recurrence and post-thrombotic complications. A 46-year-old woman who was neither an athlete nor a manual laborer presented with a four-day history of right upper-limb pain and swelling following repetitive overhead activity. She reported progressive swelling, positional bluish discoloration on arm elevation, and episodic pallor of the thumb and index finger. No secondary provoking factor for venous thromboembolism was identified. Physical examination revealed a swollen right arm with prominent superficial veins and bluish discoloration provoked within 10-15 seconds of arm elevation. Initial duplex ultrasonography identified right subclavian vein thrombosis, with the axillary and brachial veins reported as patent. However, computed tomography (CT) venography performed the following day demonstrated thrombosis involving both the right axillary and subclavian veins. CT angiography additionally demonstrated focal stenosis of the right subclavian artery at the thoracic outlet. The patient underwent catheter-directed thrombolysis followed by first rib resection for thoracic outlet decompression. This case documents PSS outside its typical demographic in a patient presenting with upper limb swelling and discoloration following repetitive overhead activity. The discordant axillary vein findings emphasize the importance of interpreting sequential vascular imaging studies in the context of their timing and modality. The accompanying episodic digital pallor and CT finding of focal subclavian arterial stenosis highlight the importance of considering possible arterial involvement in a predominantly venous presentation. Following treatment, the symptoms resolved, and venous patency was maintained at four-week follow-up.

It typically occurs in young, active individuals performing strenuous upper limb exercises and presents with pain, swelling, and discoloration of the affected limb. Early diagnosis and specialist management are important for optimizing outcomes.

title: Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Hospitalized Medical Patients: A Narrative Review of Risk Stratification, Treatment Duration, and Bleeding Trade-Offs.
abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains a leading preventable cause of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized medical patients, yet decisions about who should receive prophylaxis - and for how long - remain far from settled. This review synthesizes evidence from 22 sources, including randomized trials, prospective and retrospective cohorts, systematic reviews, and major society guidelines, addressing risk stratification, in-hospital anticoagulant prophylaxis, extended-duration direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), the associated bleeding trade-offs, and real-world implementation. The evidence broadly supports pharmacologic prophylaxis during hospitalization for appropriately selected, acutely ill medical patients with acceptable bleeding risk, with the strongest randomized evidence favoring low-molecular-weight heparin during the inpatient period. That benefit comes with trade-offs worth weighing carefully, since even well-supported regimens carry a measurable increase in bleeding risk alongside their protective effect. Commonly used risk-assessment tools have real limitations as well: the Padua and IMPROVE scores offer a useful clinical framework, but head-to-head comparison shows both discriminate poorly between patients who will and won't develop VTE, and real-world implementation data reveal frequent misclassification and inconsistent dose administration. Extended-duration anticoagulation after discharge follows a similar pattern across the major DOAC trials in this space - fewer thrombotic events, but more bleeding, without a clear survival benefit. Taken together, this evidence points toward a risk-adapted rather than protocol-driven approach: assess VTE and bleeding risk at admission, initiate appropriate inpatient prophylaxis, reassess as the clinical picture changes, confirm that prescribed doses are actually being given, and reserve extended anticoagulation after discharge for carefully selected patients rather than applying it as a default. Meaningful progress in this area will likely come less from another static risk score and more from models that can track mobility, bleeding risk, and treatment response dynamically over the course of a hospital stay.

This review synthesizes evidence from 22 sources, including randomized trials, prospective and retrospective cohorts, systematic reviews, and major society guidelines, addressing risk stratification, in-hospital anticoagulant prophylaxis, extended-duration direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), the associated bleeding trade-offs, and real-world implementation. The evidence broadly supports pharmacologic prophylaxis during hospitalization for appropriately selected, acutely ill medical patients with acceptable bleeding risk, with the strongest randomized evidence favoring low-molecular-weight heparin during the inpatient period.

title: Mechanical Thrombectomy for Pulmonary Tumor Embolism Masquerading as Bland Pulmonary Embolism: A Case Report.
abstract: Pulmonary tumor embolism (PTE) is a rare but potentially life-threatening form of non-thrombotic pulmonary embolism. Despite advancements in management, it remains a challenging entity due to its unpredictable clinical course and high mortality rate. With the advent of minimally invasive endovascular treatment modalities, the management of pulmonary embolism has witnessed a shift from systemic thrombolysis or surgical thromboarterectomy to catheter-directed thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, or pharmaco-mechanical thrombectomy, combining mechanical thrombectomy with catheter-directed thrombolysis. We report a rare case of intermediate-risk pulmonary tumor embolism managed by large-bore aspiration thrombectomy.

title: PAD as a Marker of Systemic Atherosclerosis: A Comprehensive Review of Residual Risk and Contemporary Strategies for MACE and MALE Reduction.
abstract: Background Scope: Evidence Synthesis: Conclusions: : Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is a manifestation of systemic atherosclerosis associated with substantial risks of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and major adverse limb events (MALE).This comprehensive review examines the epidemiological and pathobiological links between PAD, polyvascular disease, and residual cardiovascular and limb risk.It summarizes contemporary evidence for integrated management through antithrombotic therapy, intensive lipid lowering, blood pressure and diabetes management, smoking cessation, structured exercise, revascularization when indicated, and longitudinal surveillance. Particular attention is given to dual-pathway inhibition, non-statin lipid-lowering agents, and cardiometabolic therapies, while distinguishing established PAD-specific benefits from subgroup or emerging evidence.A phenotype-based approach integrating ischemic, bleeding, metabolic, functional, and limb-related risk is proposed to support individualized treatment and sustained vascular protection.

title: Podiatric Hospitalist: Better Care Model.
abstract: A multidisciplinary team approach has become essential to modern hospital care, bringing together professionals from different specialties to collaborate on patient management. A Podiatric Hospitalist (PH) is a board-eligible or board-certified Doctor of Podiatric Medicine dedicated to the evaluation and management of acutely hospitalized patients with foot and ankle conditions. PHs play a vital role in this collaborative model, particularly in managing different conditions affecting the foot, ankle, and the lower extremities. Beyond serving as the gatekeepers for prevention and management of diabetic foot ulcers, PHs facilitate high-quality and efficient management of diverse lower extremity disorders including infection, trauma, sport-related injuries and chronic conditions related to diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, and autoimmune disorders. We present a care model, informed by our institutional experience, that positions the PH as a consultative and co-management member of a multidisciplinary foot and ankle and limb-salvage team, with the goal of advancing high-value care that improves outcomes, cost-effectiveness, and patient satisfaction. By integrating specialized lower extremity expertise into collaborative patient management, PHs help improve patient outcomes, enhance coordination of care, and support both preventative and surgical management strategies across multiple clinical settings. This collaborative approach enhances the quality and efficiency of healthcare delivery in hospitals. As the demand for limb salvage and high-value inpatient care continues to grow, the PH represents a practical and timely addition to multidisciplinary foot and ankle care.

title: Artificial Intelligence in 3D Aortic CTA Segmentation for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Management: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) is the reference imaging modality for diagnosis, endovascular planning, and surveillance of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs), but conventional assessment remains time-consuming, operator-dependent, and limited by complex anatomy. This narrative review examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in three-dimensional aortic CTA segmentation for AAA management. The narrative synthesis drew on literature identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and the Cochrane Library, with the original search covering January 2000 to July 2026. Ten primary studies from the existing bibliography were characterized in a study-level table, and reported Dice coefficients were displayed for nine studies. Current evidence indicates that AI-based segmentation, particularly using convolutional neural networks, U-Net-derived models, and nnU-Net frameworks, can improve the speed and reproducibility of aortic lumen, wall, thrombus, branch vessel, endograft, and aneurysm sac delineation. These techniques may support more accurate morphometric measurements, device sizing, procedural planning, quantitative surveillance, and the development of advanced imaging biomarkers. However, available studies remain heterogeneous in datasets, anatomical evaluation, imaging protocols, validation strategies, and reported performance metrics, limiting direct comparison and clinical generalizability. AI-assisted 3D segmentation represents a promising tool for transforming CTA from descriptive imaging into quantitative decision support, but robust multicenter validation, workflow integration, and expert supervision remain essential before widespread clinical adoption.

title: Falls in the elderly: under-appreciated serious sequela. A narrative review.
abstract: Ground-level falls are highly prevalent in elderly patients, and are often recurrent. Serious fractures and brain injury are common. Other types of fall-associated harm may be largely under-recognized. We reviewed PubMed (English, last 50 years) using pre-defined key-words, and reference lists to identify relevant studies. A wide spectrum of potential harm was identified and classified into five domains: thoracic injury; internal abdominal injury; vascular events (cardiac, stroke, blood vessels, venous thromboembolism); herpesviruses reactivation; and psychological impact. All were found to be infrequent or rare (excepting psychological impact), associated with delayed recognition, and significantly increased morbidity and mortality. Thus, clinicians attending geriatric patients after an accidental fall need to be more aware of the potential of a wide spectrum of complications in several domains, extending well beyond the regularly evaluated fractures and brain injury. Point of care "pan-CT" may be warranted since its sensitivity is considerably more than physical examination and radiography. Results may uncover clinically-significant occult findings, albeit unusual. Post-discharge follow up must take into account the profound psychological impact of falls on the patients.

title: Selective endovascular aortic repair in connective tissue disease patients within a multidisciplinary program achieves comparable outcomes in high-risk patients.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Endovascular aortic repair (ENDO) in patients with connective tissue disease (CTD) has historically been discouraged in society guidelines because of durability concerns. However, high-volume aortic centers increasingly employ ENDO strategies in carefully selected high-risk patients across scenarios such as rupture, dissection-related pathology, or hostile anatomy. Herein, we describe temporal ENDO adoption at our multidisciplinary CTD aortic program. METHODS: In this study, 92 patients with CTD undergoing aortic intervention at a single high-volume aortic center between 2005 and 2023 were analyzed. Patients were stratified by ENDO (n = 50) vs open repair (OPEN; n = 42). The primary outcome was freedom from aortic-related mortality (ARM). The secondary outcomes included technical success, complications, secondary aortic intervention (SAI), and overall survival. A prespecified contemporary analysis (2018-2023) was conducted to evaluate the outcomes following the establishment of a multidisciplinary CTD aortic program. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate survival and freedom from SAI. RESULTS: The mean age was 48 ± 16 years, and 34% (n = 31) were female. Diagnoses included Marfan syndrome (69%), Loeys-Dietz syndrome (15%), familial aortopathy (11%), and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (5%). Patients who underwent ENDO more frequently had prior sternotomy/open cardiac surgery (68% vs 19%; P < .0001), prior aortic surgery (70% vs 33%; P = .0007), and urgent presentation (50% vs 14%; P = .0004). Overall, 60% of these patients were deemed unfit for open repair by the multidisciplinary aortic team because of physiologic risk, anatomic complexity, or urgent presentation. The technical success rate was lower after ENDO (82% vs 98%; P = .02), and the 30-day reintervention rate was higher (16% vs 0%; P = .01). The median follow-up period was 2.3 years [interquartile range, 1.1-4.7]. SAIs occurred more frequently following ENDO (56% vs 12%; P = .0001), including planned staged procedures (ENDO: 28.6% vs OPEN: 20%; P = 1) and unplanned reinterventions (ENDO: 71.4% vs OPEN: 80%; P = 1). In the full cohort, patients undergoing ENDO had lower 3-year survival rates (71% ± 7% vs 92% ± 4%; log-rank P = .03). In the contemporary cohort, survival at 2 years following ENDO (n = 17) was poorer than that after OPEN (n = 42), although the difference did not reach significance (71% ± 14% vs 92% ± 4%; log-rank P = .1). Similarly, the rate of freedom from ARM was lower, but not significantly different (88% ± 12% vs 98% ± 2%; log-rank P = .4). CONCLUSIONS: Open repair remains the gold standard for connective tissue disease-associated aortic disease. In carefully selected high-risk patients, ENDO serves as a complementary strategy with acceptable contemporary survival and comparable freedom from ARM. Higher secondary intervention rates reflect both planned staged repair and unplanned surveillance-detected failure modes, underscoring the need for lifelong follow-up within multidisciplinary programs.

However, high-volume aortic centers increasingly employ ENDO strategies in carefully selected high-risk patients across scenarios such as rupture, dissection-related pathology, or hostile anatomy. Herein, we describe temporal ENDO adoption at our multidisciplinary CTD aortic program.

title: Impact of Undertreated Antithrombotic Therapy on Adverse Patient Outcomes: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association.
abstract: Antithrombotic therapy undertreatment includes omission, nonadherence, underdosing, and clinical circumstances that result in subtherapeutic antithrombotic levels. Antithrombotic undertreatment has profound implications for patient safety, public health, and healthcare costs. Due to deviation from evidence-based clinical practice, misperceptions of bleeding versus thrombotic risk, and inequities in healthcare access, many patients with atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism, or peripheral artery disease remain untreated or receive suboptimal anticoagulant dosing. Antithrombotic undertreatment has been shown to increase rates of ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, recurrent thrombosis, and mortality. Real-world data continue to highlight substantial gaps in care, which appear to be magnified in patients with inequity in social determinants of health. The emergence of antithrombotic stewardship, in concert with growing bodies of literature on antithrombotic agent underdosing, represents a transformative opportunity to address these gaps through structured, interprofessional, and evidence-based approaches. Through interdisciplinary collaboration, healthcare professionals are well positioned to enhance patient health and safety by recognizing and recommitting to reducing antithrombotic undertreatment.

title: Beyond the Threshold: Continuous Creatinine Change and Outcomes After Endovascular Thrombectomy for Acute Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI) after endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) worsens outcomes in acute ischemic stroke, but threshold-based definitions do not capture prognostic information from subthreshold changes. We tested whether early creatinine change within 48 hours of EVT conveys graded prognostic information beyond dichotomous CA-AKI. METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of the CAN-REST registry (Contrast-Associated Nephropathy After Endovascular Stroke Treatment), a retrospective multicenter observational cohort study of 6638 EVT-treated adults with acute ischemic stroke enrolled at 73 centers in 16 countries between January 1 and December 31, 2023. Early creatinine change was quantified as the natural logarithm ratio of 48-hour creatinine to baseline creatinine (ln[48-hour/baseline creatinine]), with CA-AKI defined per Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes criteria (≥0.3 mg/dL or ≥1.5× baseline rise within 48 hours). Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for prespecified baseline and periprocedural covariates examined associations with 90-day modified Rankin Scale shift and in-hospital mortality; linear versus restricted cubic spline specification was selected by likelihood ratio testing, and contrasts were estimated at ±10%, ±25%, and ±50%. RESULTS: Greater creatinine worsening within 48 hours of EVT was independently associated with an unfavorable 90-day modified Rankin Scale shift (adjusted common odds ratio per 1-unit log-ratio increase, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.07-2.04]; linear) and in-hospital mortality (nonlinear dose-response, of larger magnitude). A 10% increase in creatinine at 48 hours-well below Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes threshold-was associated with worse functional outcome (adjusted common odds ratio, 1.04 [95% CI, 1.01-1.07]) and death (adjusted odds ratio, 1.22 [95% CI, 1.13-1.32]); a 10% decrease in creatinine at 48 hours was associated with lower odds of both outcomes (adjusted common odds ratio, 0.96 [95% CI, 0.93-0.99]; adjusted odds ratio, 0.74 [95% CI, 0.65-0.86]). The functional-outcome association concentrated at upper modified Rankin Scale cut-points (severe disability, death); effect modification by baseline renal function was not significant. CONCLUSIONS: Early creatinine change after EVT conveys graded, outcome-specific prognostic information extending below formal CA-AKI thresholds, with a dose-response detectable at changes as modest as ±10%, complementing binary CA-AKI as a framework for post-EVT renal risk assessment. title: Artificial intelligence for the detection of large vessel occlusion stroke and workflow optimization: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: To evaluate the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) tools on workflow efficiency, treatment times, and clinical outcomes in patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke. METHODS: We included observational studies that assessed the implementation of AI-based tools in the management of patients with suspected or confirmed LVO stroke. Eligible studies reported workflow, treatment, safety, or functional outcomes. Data were extracted on thrombolysis rates, CTA-to-arterial puncture time, door-to-puncture time, endovascular treatment (EVT) access, reperfusion success, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH), mortality, and functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days. Random-effects models were applied to calculate pooled mean differences (MD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: Thirteen studies were included. AI implementation significantly reduced workflow delays: CTA-to-puncture time decreased by -40.20 minutes (95% CI -66.41 to -13.99; P<0.01) and door-to-puncture time by -23.17 minutes (95% CI -38.71 to -7.63; P<0.01). Thrombolysis administration showed no difference (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.57-1.09; P=0.15). Similarly, no significant effects were observed for EVT access (RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.66-1.44; P=0.89), reperfusion success (RR 1.06; 95% CI 1.00-1.12; P=0.06), sICH (RR 0.63; 95% CI 0.30-1.35; P=0.23), or mortality (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.38-1.37; P=0.32). However, AI-based workflows significantly improved functional independence at 90 days (RR 1.55; 95% CI 1.12-2.15; P=0.008). CONCLUSIONS: AI tools significantly improve treatment times and functional independence in acute LVO stroke without increasing adverse events.

METHODS: We included observational studies that assessed the implementation of AI-based tools in the management of patients with suspected or confirmed LVO stroke. Eligible studies reported workflow, treatment, safety, or functional outcomes.

title: Long-Term Complications and Secondary Procedures After Open Reduction and Internal Fixation of Ankle Fractures: A Descriptive Epidemiologic Study of Over 50,000 Patients.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ankle fractures account for ~10% of fractures, ~40% treated operatively, yet absolute long-horizon complication and secondary-procedure estimates by fracture pattern and comorbidity remain limited. Prior series generally left decedents in the denominator as though still at risk. METHODS: Retrospective cohort study of aggregated, de-identified TriNetX data. Adults (≥18 years) undergoing operative ankle fracture fixation (2000-2015) were assigned to four fracture-pattern cohorts (isolated lateral, medial, bimalleolar, trimalleolar) and described across five overlapping comorbidity strata (diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, liver disease, renal failure, open fracture) plus a no-comorbidity reference. Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence, with death as the competing event, was estimated for 90-day infection, venous thromboembolism (VTE), and mortality, and for nonunion/malunion repair, clinically attended arthritis, conversion to arthrodesis/arthroplasty, and hardware removal at 2, 5, and 10 years. No hypothesis was tested or comparison performed. RESULTS: Of 68,992 eligible adults, 56,724 carried no qualifying comorbidity codes (lateral 18,871; bimalleolar 16,794; trimalleolar 13,058; medial 8,001); 12,268 carried ≥1. In reference cohorts, 90-day cumulative incidence was 1.93-2.28% (infection), 1.61-2.19% (VTE), and 0.30-0.75% (mortality); comorbidity-stratum maxima were 9.61%, 8.62%, and 4.15%. At 10 years, reference-cohort cumulative incidence was 17.10-20.20% (clinically attended arthritis), 11.69-14.32% (hardware removal), 0.32-1.73% (nonunion/malunion repair), and 0.48-1.62% (arthrodesis/arthroplasty conversion), reaching 22.60% and 6.34% in comorbidity strata. Cumulative deaths by 10 years reached 29.2% (trimalleolar renal-failure stratum) versus 2.8-4.7% in the reference cohorts. CONCLUSION: Competing-risks cumulative incidence of coded complications and secondary procedures after ankle ORIF is reported by fracture pattern and comorbidity stratum. These unadjusted estimates support no comparison between patterns or strata but provide reference figures for preoperative counseling and for designing adjusted patient-level studies. # Level of Evidence IV, retrospective descriptive epidemiologic study. Keywords: ankle fracture; open reduction internal fixation; competing risks; cumulative incidence; clinically attended post-traumatic arthritis; administrative database.

Prior series generally left decedents in the denominator as though still at risk. METHODS: Retrospective cohort study of aggregated, de-identified TriNetX data.

title: Ovarian Vein Thrombosis: Diagnosis and Management of an Unusual-Site Venous Thrombosis for the Acute Physician.
abstract: Ovarian vein thrombosis (OVT) is a rare and under-recognised form of venous thromboembolism that is frequently missed due to absent or non-specific symptoms. Consequently, diagnosis is often delayed or made incidentally on cross-sectional imaging. Although OVT is usually associated with the postpartum period, it is increasingly recognised in patients with malignancy, pelvic surgery, and intra-abdominal infection. Potential complications may be life-threatening and include thrombus extension, pulmonary embolism, and, less commonly, sepsis and bleeding. Despite increasing recognition, evidence remains limited to small case series and reports. As such, there remains uncertainty regarding the optimal diagnostic approach and the use of anticoagulation, including indications for anticoagulation, duration of treatment, and follow-up. This review summarises the current evidence on the epidemiology, risk factors, clinical presentation, investigations, and management of OVT, and proposes a practical approach to the diagnosis and treatment of OVT for the acute physician.

title: Endoluminal Reconstruction of Complex Cervical Internal Carotid Artery Dissections Using the Surpass Elite Flow Diverter: A Technical Report.
abstract: Most cervical internal carotid artery (ICA) dissections heal with antithrombotic therapy. Complex lesions with flow-limiting stenosis, multisegment involvement, or persistent wide-necked pseudoaneurysms may fail medical management and require endovascular reconstruction, the indications for which remain individualized. Conventional carotid stents conform poorly to acute curves. Flow diverters reconstruct the parent lumen and accommodate angulation, but cervical use is off-label and experience with current-generation devices is limited. To our knowledge, we report the first use of the Surpass Elite flow diverter (Stryker Neurovascular, Fremont, CA) for cervical ICA dissection, in two patients, as the primary scaffold within hybrid constructs supported by coil embolization, angioplasty, and carotid stenting. An 18-year-old female with a Biffl grade III blunt injury had a right cervical dissection with critical narrowing of the true lumen and two large wide-necked pseudoaneurysms persisting despite antiplatelet therapy; coil embolization of both sacs, a single flow diverter, angioplasty, and telescoped carotid stents restored luminal caliber, with six-month angiography showing complete resolution without coil compaction. A 72-year-old male with a prior left middle cerebral artery infarct had a 6-cm chronic dissection of the cervical left ICA with dense distal calcification, aneurysmal dilatation, 70% stenosis, and angiographic hypoperfusion; two telescoped flow diverters and a carotid stent reconstructed the lumen without residual stenosis. Both patients received dual antiplatelet therapy starting seven days preoperatively, with P2Y12 reaction units verified within the target range, and neither had periprocedural complications. Reconstruction with the Surpass Elite within a hybrid construct was technically feasible in these two contrasting morphologies; two cases cannot establish efficacy, and the independent contribution of the device cannot be determined.

Complex lesions with flow-limiting stenosis, multisegment involvement, or persistent wide-necked pseudoaneurysms may fail medical management and require endovascular reconstruction, the indications for which remain individualized. Conventional carotid stents conform poorly to acute curves.

title: Severe Rhabdomyolysis With Minimal Muscular Symptoms After Long-Term Rosuvastatin Use: A Case Report and Brief Literature Review.
abstract: Severe rhabdomyolysis may present with limited muscular symptoms despite substantial biochemical injury. We describe a case of suspected statin-associated rhabdomyolysis during prolonged rosuvastatin exposure. A 65-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, peripheral arterial disease requiring bilateral below-knee amputations, and previous rhabdomyolysis presented with generalized weakness, abdominal discomfort, and left flank pain. He had taken rosuvastatin for more than 10 years. Admission investigations demonstrated creatine kinase of 23,107 U/L, creatinine of 7.80 mg/dL, markedly elevated aminotransferases, and brown urine. Creatine kinase subsequently peaked at 38,747 U/L despite limited muscular complaints. Progressive azotemia and encephalopathy prompted hemodialysis. Rosuvastatin was discontinued, and supportive treatment was provided without immunosuppression. The reported myositis panel was negative, while magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated mild, nonspecific muscle edema. By discharge, weakness and encephalopathy had resolved, strength was preserved on focused examination, and creatine kinase had decreased to 1,003 U/L. The patient was advised to avoid all statins. Outpatient hemodialysis, rheumatology follow-up, and serial creatine kinase measurements were arranged, with anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibody testing and muscle biopsy planned if creatine kinase remained persistently elevated after discharge. This case highlights the discrepancy between biochemical severity and muscular symptoms during long-standing statin exposure. Improvement after statin withdrawal and supportive care supported a suspected statin-associated process but did not establish causality or exclude an autoimmune mechanism. Continued clinical and biochemical follow-up was essential to document recovery and determine the need for further investigation.
englishSummary: Severe rhabdomyolysis may present with limited muscular symptoms despite substantial biochemical injury. We describe a case of suspected statin-associated rhabdomyolysis during prolonged rosuvastatin exposure. A 65-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, peripheral arterial disease requiring bilateral below-knee amputations, and previous rhabdomyolysis presented with generalized weakness, abdominal discomfort, and left flank pain.

title: Catastrophic High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism With Recurrent Cardiac Arrest Successfully Treated With Rescue Mechanical Thrombectomy After Systemic Thrombolysis.
abstract: High-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) complicated by cardiac arrest carries an extremely high mortality, and the optimal rescue strategy after an inadequate response to systemic thrombolysis remains uncertain. We report the case of a 53-year-old woman with previous deep-vein thrombosis who was admitted after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and subsequently experienced three additional episodes of cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography demonstrated extensive bilateral central PE with severe right ventricular dilation and interventricular septal shift. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase was administered. Despite thrombolysis and vasopressor/inotropic support, persistent cardiogenic-obstructive shock, electrical instability, and severe right ventricular pressure overload remained. Approximately 4 h after thrombolysis, rescue mechanical aspiration thrombectomy was performed using the Indigo® Aspiration System with Lightning Flash™ (Penumbra, Inc., Alameda, CA, USA). Ultrasound-guided right common femoral venous access was obtained with an 18 F sheath, and aspiration was performed in both pulmonary arteries. Pulmonary artery pressure decreased from 34 mmHg before aspiration to 25 mmHg at the end of the procedure. The patient subsequently achieved progressive hemodynamic stabilization. After prolonged mechanical ventilation and tracheostomy, neurological recovery was favorable. At discharge, echocardiography showed normal biventricular systolic function. This case illustrates that prompt escalation to rescue mechanical thrombectomy may be considered in selected patients with high-risk PE when shock, electrical instability, and right ventricular overload persist despite systemic thrombolysis.

We report the case of a 53-year-old woman with previous deep-vein thrombosis who was admitted after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and subsequently experienced three additional episodes of cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography demonstrated extensive bilateral central PE with severe right ventricular dilation and interventricular septal shift.

title: AngioJet rheolytic thrombectomy under superior vena cava filter protection for acute upper extremity deep vein thrombosis in patients with cancer: a single-center, retrospective analysis.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: The incidence of upper extremity deep vein thrombosis (UEDVT) is increasing, and percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy (PMT) is receiving more attention as a treatment option. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy and clinical outcomes of PMT combined with superior vena cava (SVC) filter protection in cancer patients with acute UEDVT. METHODS: This study included all patients with acute UEDVT who underwent treatment with an 8-Fr AngioJet thrombectomy system (Boston Scientific) under the protection of a retrievable SVC filter between January 1, 2020, and October 1, 2025. The evaluation indicators included technical success rate (defined as a thrombus clearance rate >80%), intraoperative adverse events, degree of limb swelling relief, incidence of pulmonary embolism, and thrombus recurrence during follow-up. RESULTS: A total of 19 patients (10 female; mean age 60.84 ± 11.30 years) were included. All patients had secondary UEDVT and a history of malignant tumors, with 14 cases (73.7%) having a history of central venous catheterization. All procedures achieved technical success, with no severe adverse events such as major bleeding occurring intraoperatively, nor were there any new symptomatic pulmonary embolisms. The average circumference of the affected limb 10 cm above the elbow before surgery was 29.83 ± 2.20 cm, which decreased to 26.98 ± 2.0 cm on the second postoperative day. During the 6-month follow-up, one patient with advanced lung cancer developed swelling of the upper limb on postoperative day 136, confirmed by ultrasound to be a recurrence of deep vein thrombosis; another patient was found to have an asymptomatic mural thrombus on ultrasound examination on postoperative day 28. CONCLUSION: PMT with the 8-Fr AngioJet system and SVC filter protection appears to be a safe and effective treatment option for cancer patients with acute UEDVT.
englishSummary: OBJECTIVE: The incidence of upper extremity deep vein thrombosis (UEDVT) is increasing, and percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy (PMT) is receiving more attention as a treatment option. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy and clinical outcomes of PMT combined with superior vena cava (SVC) filter protection in cancer patients with acute UEDVT. METHODS: This study included all patients with acute UEDVT who underwent treatment with an 8-Fr AngioJet thrombectomy system (Boston Scientific) under the protection of a retrievable SVC filter between January 1, 2020, and October 1, 2025.

title: Perioperative Lactate, Survival, and Complications Following Lung Transplantation.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To examine perioperative lactate and its association with survival and postoperative complications following lung transplantation (LTx). DESIGN: Single-center retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Academic tertiary-care transplant center. PARTICIPANTS: Adult patients undergoing LTx between February 2018 and January 2023. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Serum lactate was measured at 6-hour intervals from the start of surgery, and the maximum value within the first 0 to 6 hours was recorded. Patients were categorized into the high-lactate group (upper quartile, ≥4.2 mmol/L) and low-lactate group (lower 3 quartiles). Primary outcomes were 1-year and overall survival. Secondary outcomes included renal failure, venous thromboembolism (VTE), primary graft dysfunction grade 3 (PGD3), mechanical ventilation duration, intensive care unit (ICU) and post-transplant length of stay, and in-hospital mortality. Among 225 recipients (median age, 62.3 years; 34.2% female), high lactate was not associated with 1-year or overall survival. However, recipients with high lactate had higher rates of PGD3 at 72 hours (42.1% v 13.1%, p < 0.001), longer mechanical ventilation duration (3 days v 2 days, p = 0.003), longer ICU stay (11.6 days v 7 days, p = 0.013), and higher in-hospital mortality rate (7% v 0.6%, p = 0.019). No significant differences were observed in renal failure, VTE, or post-transplant length of stay. CONCLUSIONS: Elevated perioperative serum lactate was associated with PGD3 at 72 hours, prolonged mechanical ventilation, longer ICU stay, and in-hospital mortality but not 1-year or overall survival following LTx. These findings suggest that perioperative lactate may aid in identifying high-risk patients early in their postoperative course despite its lack of association with long-term survival.

title: Hemodynamic Analysis of Modified Splenic Arteriovenous Shunt in Pancreas Transplantation.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of a modified splenic arteriovenous shunt technique in pancreas transplantation through intraoperative hemodynamic monitoring and postoperative follow-up. METHODS: A total of 12 patients undergoing simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplantation were enrolled. Under three consecutive intraoperative states (spleen preserved, splenic arteriovenous clamped, and splenic arteriovenous shunt created), color Doppler ultrasound was used to measure peak systolic velocity (PS) and volumetric flow (VF) of the splenic artery and vein at the same point in the distal pancreatic tail, while portal venous pressure was recorded using an intravascular pressure transducer. Postoperative graft function, thrombotic events, and complications were regularly followed up. RESULTS: Compared with the spleen-preserved state, the clamped state showed significant reductions in splenic arterial PS and VF (15.24 ± 4.43 cm/s, 16.62 ± 6.84 mL/min) and splenic venous PS and VF (16.31 ± 3.82 cm/s, 60.32 ± 16.07 mL/min) (P < 0.001). In the shunt state, splenic arterial (54.47 ± 3.45 cm/s, 157.39 ± 11.24 mL/min) and venous (49.27 ± 6.61 cm/s, 177.89 ± 14.15 mL/min) flow parameters showed no significant differences compared with the spleen-preserved state (P > 0.05), but were significantly higher than those in the clamped state (P < 0.001). Portal venous pressure showed no significant differences among the three states (P > 0.05). At a median follow-up of 5 months, no graft thrombosis, pancreatitis, or gastrointestinal bleeding was observed, and patient and graft survival rates were both 100% at the last follow-up. Glycated hemoglobin decreased from 7.37% ± 0.68% preoperatively to 5.81% ± 0.32% (P < 0.005), and left ventricular ejection fraction increased from 59.50% ± 3.23% to 67.33% ± 2.84% (P < 0.005). CONCLUSION: The modified splenic arteriovenous shunt maintains physiological perfusion of the pancreatic allograft without elevating portal venous pressure, and may mitigate the hypoperfusion and blood stasis associated with conventional splenic vessel ligation. Based on the short-term results of this study, this modified technique appears safe and feasible, and may contribute to reducing early thrombotic complications after pancreas transplantation.

title: Vascular Management Strategies and Outcomes of Infectious Arterial Complications Involving the Kidney Transplant Vasculature: A Systematic Review and Evidence-Informed Treatment Framework.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Infectious arterial complications involving the kidney transplant (KT) vasculature are rare but life-threatening and frequently result in KT loss. The lack of evidence-based guidance for vascular management strategies underscores the need for systematic synthesis to inform clinical decision-making. METHODS: A systematic search was performed from database inception through August 22, 2025, for reports of culture-proven infectious vascular complications-including arterial rupture, detachment, pseudoaneurysm, aneurysm, thrombosis, or stenosis-involving the transplant renal artery, iliac vessels, or arterial anastomosis in KT recipients. Eligible studies reported vascular management strategies. Due to methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively using proportion-based comparisons. RESULTS: Eighty reports (1972-2025) comprising 139 cases were included. Candida species were most frequent, followed by Pseudomonas, Aspergillus, and Staphylococcus species. Pseudoaneurysm and arterial rupture were the predominant clinical presentation, typically occuring within the first month after transplantation. Outcome patterns differed by transplant nephrectomy status, with vascular management strategies performed without transplant nephrectomy demonstrating higher reported proportions of uneventful follow-up. Autologous interposition grafting demonstrated the most favorable outcome pattern (86.7% uneventful recovery; 6.7% reintervention and mortality), even when transplant nephrectomy is unavoidable. Covered stent placement was the most frequently reported intervention andshowed favorable outcomes in selected KT-preserving cases (75% uneventful recovery). Primary surgical repair had the highest reintervention proportion (59.1%), whereas arterial ligation had the highest mortality (43.8%) and accounted for all reported limb loss. CONCLUSION: Across five decades of case-based evidence, autologous interposition grafting demonstrated the most favorable outcome pattern and may represent the preferred vascular management strategy when durable arterial reconstruction is feasible, including when transplant nephrectomy is required. Covered stent placement may provide a useful option in selected cases or as a temporizing strategy for hemorrhage control. These findings should guide rather than define management decisions given the heterogeneous evidence base. HIGHLIGHTS: First systematic synthesis of management strategies for infectious arterial complications involving the kidney transplant vasculature Candida was the most frequently reported pathogen; pseudoaneurysm and arterial rupture were the predominant presentations Vascular management strategies performed without transplant nephrectomy demonstrated higher reported proportions of uneventful follow-up Autologous interposition grafting showed the most favorable reported outcome pattern, even when transplant nephrectomy is unavoidable Ligation and primary repair were associated with higher reported mortality and reintervention, respectively.

The lack of evidence-based guidance for vascular management strategies underscores the need for systematic synthesis to inform clinical decision-making. title: PGC1α/SIRT3-Mediated Oxidative Stress and Downregulation of NLRP3 Expression by Sodium Thiosulfate Pre- and Post-Treatment Accelerates Recovery from Ischemia-Reperfusion-Induced Acute Kidney Injury.
abstract: Background: Methods: Results: Conclusions: p p p p p p Renal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) is the leading cause of acute kidney injury (AKI). It is associated with reduced blood flow as encountered in vascular surgery, including aortic aneurysm repair and kidney transplantation. In this study, we investigated whether pre- and/or post-administration of sodium thiosulfate (STS), an FDA-approved hydrogen sulfide donor drug, attenuated IRI-induced AKI in rats.AKI was induced in male rats by clamping both renal arteries for 60 min. At 30 min before clamping, and 30 min after reperfusion, STS was administered at a weigh-based dose to achieve a circulating concentration of 150 μM, after which the rats were kept in metabolic cages for urine and blood collection on postoperative days (POD) 3, 5, and 7. Rats were sacrificed on POD3, POD5, and POD7, and kidneys were harvested for analysis. Sham-operated rats received no treatment.AKI was evidenced by markedly higher acute tubular necrosis score, and renal protein and gene expression of damage markers (KIM-1 and NGAL), as well as markers of oxidative stress (MDA, GSH, and SOD), inflammation (MPO, IL-6), and apoptosis (TUNEL). While significant incremental improvement was observed in the expression of these markers in the pre-treatment only and post-treatment only groups over the POD3-7 observation period compared to untreated control group (< 0.05), superior renal protection was observed in the pre + post-treatment group (< 0.01). Functionally, serum creatinine levels were significantly higher over the POD3-7 observation period in the untreated group relative to pre-treatment and post-treatment groups (< 0.05), and markedly lower in the pre + post-treatment group (< 0.001), which positively correlated with urine output. Urine osmolality was statistically similar to sham-operated rats on POD5 and 7, while all other groups showed decreased urine osmolality on POD3 and 5 (< 0.05). Mechanistically, the protective effect of STS correlated with upregulation of PGC1α and SIRT3 protein and gene expression and downregulation of NLRP3 protein and mRNA expression in the pre + post-treatment group compared to other groups (< 0.05).The present study reports for the first time the protective effect of STS against IRI-induced AKI, and indicates PGC1α, SIRT3, and NLRP3 as molecular targets of STS.

title: Intended Thrombectomy for Basilar Artery Occlusion with Mild Deficits: Evidence from a Multicenter Prospective Registry.
abstract: P Supplemental material is available for this article. Background The role of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) in basilar artery occlusion (BAO) with mild deficits (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS] score < 10) remains uncertain. Purpose To compare the outcomes of EVT combined with best medical management (BMM) versus BMM alone in individuals with BAO and mild deficits. Materials and Methods Consecutive eligible patients treated at eight stroke centers between September 2023 and March 2025 were enrolled in a prospective registry. The primary outcome was 90-day functional independence (modified Rankin Scale [mRS] score of 0-2). Secondary outcomes were 90-day excellent outcome (mRS score of 0-1), death, and early neurologic deterioration (END), defined as a four-point or greater increase in NIHSS score within 72 hours. Primary analyses followed an intention-to-treat-like framework with inverse probability weighting (IPW). As-treated and per-protocol sensitivity analyses were used to assess the robustness of the results and the impact of treatment crossover (EVT after END). Results Among 401 participants (mean age, 64.9 years ± 8.9 [SD]; 278 male participants), the median onset-to-arterial-puncture time in the EVT group was 402 minutes (IQR, 271-583 minutes). After multivariable adjustment in the IPW-adjusted data, EVT was associated with higher odds of functional independence (odds ratio [OR], 1.55 [95% CI: 1.17, 2.06]) and excellent outcome (OR, 1.48 [95% CI: 1.09, 2.03]) and lower odds of death (OR, 0.65 [95% CI: 0.45, 0.77]) and END (OR, 0.35 [95% CI: 0.20, 0.61]). Subgroup analyses demonstrated EVT-related functional benefit in participants with NIHSS scores of 6-9 but not in those with NIHSS scores of 0-5 (for interaction = .02 for functional independence); however, in participants with NIHSS scores of 0-5, EVT was associated with lower odds of END and death. Sensitivity analyses accounting for treatment crossover showed attenuated functional advantage for EVT. Conclusion In participants with BAO and mild deficits, EVT plus BMM was associated with better outcomes than BMM alone; however, functional benefit was observed in those with NIHSS scores of 6-9 but not those with NIHSS scores of 0-5. title: Case 351: Thalamic Dementia Secondary to Dural Arteriovenous Fistula.
abstract: A 76-year-old man with a medical history of diabetes, hypertension, and dilated cardiomyopathy developed new symptoms of confusion, repeated falls, and urinary incontinence over the course of 3-4 months, which worsened over a 2-week period, leading to presentation at the emergency room. His partner reported that before this, he had no memory or movement disorders, but now he was experiencing memory lapses, such as forgetting his mother's recent death, and functional cognitive problems, including an inability to remember how to perform tasks that were previously simple for him, such as dosing his insulin with meals. At presentation, the patient was awake and alert, oriented to his name and location but not to the date. Full neurologic examinations, including of the motor and sensory systems and cranial nerves, were normal. There were no signs of meningism, no fever or leukocytosis, and no history of recent travel. Serum electrolyte panel and thiamine levels were normal, and he had no history of alcohol or drug abuse. Initial evaluation included noncontrast CT of the head, the results of which prompted multiphasic CT angiography of the head including parenchymal phase imaging and admission for observation and monitoring with serial noncontrast CT of the head. The patient's symptoms worsened during his hospital stay. He also developed facial twitching, increased drowsiness, and seizure episodes. He was therefore evaluated with noncontrast MRI of the brain and then digital subtraction angiography with external carotid artery and internal carotid artery contrast agent injections.

title: Complication Prevention in Combined Abdominoplasty and Gynecologic Procedures: A Multidisciplinary Narrative Review.
abstract: P Level of Evidence: Combined abdominoplasty (ABP) and open gynecologic surgery is an established approach that may reduce anesthesia exposure, shorten convalescence, and lower costs relative to staged procedures, yet its safety profile and optimal perioperative management remain incompletely defined, with a heterogeneous evidence base and no updated synthesis since 2007. The authors conducted a narrative review, searching PubMed, MEDLINE, and Scopus from inception to March 2026 for studies of combined open ABP and gynecologic procedures in adults; 14 studies published between 1983 and 2022 were included, comprising retrospective cohorts, case series, case-control, and observational studies, 1 literature review, and 2 case reports (sample sizes 1-269). Reported outcomes were heterogeneous: some early series described longer operative times and greater morbidity, whereas recent comparative data found combined ABP-hysterectomy associated with a complication rate comparable to or lower than staged surgery (7.7% vs 12.5%;= .04) alongside reduced operative and anesthesia times. Key modifiable risk factors include smoking, obesity, and the American Society of Anesthesiologists class. Formal venous thromboembolism risk stratification using the Caprini model with risk-adjusted prophylaxis, prophylactic antibiotics, maintenance of normothermia, separate instrument sets, and coordinated multidisciplinary planning are the principal evidence-based strategies for complication prevention. Rare delayed complications, notably abdominal-wall endometrioma, are consistently missed by short-term follow-up. Combined ABP and open gynecologic surgery can be performed safely in appropriately selected patients, although the evidence is limited by retrospective designs and outcome heterogeneity; prospective multicenter studies with standardized reporting and long-term follow-up are needed.3 (Therapeutic) For image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.

title: Stroke and Bleeding Risk in Long-Term Care Residents With Atrial Fibrillation Who Discontinue Anticoagulation.
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Atrial fibrillation (AF) leads to more than 100 000 cases of stroke yearly and is particularly prevalent in long-term care (LTC) residents. Anticoagulation (AC) is the mainstay of stroke prevention, but given its risks, clinicians and residents may consider discontinuation at the time of LTC entry. OBJECTIVE: To estimate the association between AC discontinuation and stroke and bleeding risk among LTC residents with AF. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This comparative effectiveness research study with target trial emulation used claims data (2020-2021) from LTC facilities in the US serving Medicare beneficiaries. Medicare beneficiaries with AF receiving AC who entered LTC between April 1 and December 31, 2020, were included; those with additional indications for AC, including prosthetic heart valve or venous thromboembolism, were excluded. Analysis was performed in August 2026. EXPOSURE: Discontinuer vs continuer assignment. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The main outcomes were stroke (including ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack, and systemic embolism) and bleeding, assessed using Medicare claims. A target trial emulation was conducted with clone censor weighting (CCW) analysis. Specifically, eligible LTC residents were assigned (cloned) to each of 2 strategies: AC discontinuation or AC continuation. Clones were then censored when they deviated from their assigned strategy, and inverse probability of censoring weighting was applied to address informative censoring: residents who deviated differing systematically from those who did not. Subdistribution hazard ratios (sHRs) for stroke and bleeding were then calculated to account for competing mortality and a cause-specific hazard ratio (HR) for death. RESULTS: This study included 15 426 LTC residents (mean [SD] age, 82.6 [7.6] years). Most were female (62.6%). AC discontinuers had 187 strokes, 297 bleeding events, and 3684 deaths over a mean (SD) of 128.9 (177.9) days. AC continuers had 321 strokes, 493 bleeding events, and 5475 deaths over a mean (SD) of 279.6 (204.9) days. Discontinuers had similar stroke risk (sHR, 1.07; 95% CI, 0.93-1.23) and bleeding risk (sHR, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.92-1.13) compared with continuers, but discontinuers had higher mortality risk (HR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.23-1.31). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this target trial emulation with CCW in a cohort of LTC residents with AF, AC discontinuation was not associated with higher stroke or bleeding risk. Very high mortality, unmeasured confounding, and reliance on claims-based outcome ascertainment may have limited the ability to better understand the consequences of AC discontinuation on stroke and bleeding.

OBJECTIVE: To estimate the association between AC discontinuation and stroke and bleeding risk among LTC residents with AF.

title: A single-cell census of pulmonary endarterectomies tissue across different anatomical regions in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA) remains one of potentially curative options for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). The operation can remove proximal thromboembolic materials and their secondary branches. However, the cellular landscape and pathological features across different anatomical regions remain limited understood. METHODS: Ten patients with CTEPH undergoing PEA surgery and six reference distal pulmonary arteries were conducted single-cell transcriptomics to profile the cellular composition of the main and its bifurcate portion. RESULTS: Pronounced muscularised and fibrotic thrombi organisation were presented in the main portion, and the proportion of mononuclear phagocytes was significantly increased. Inflammatory response and pro-inflammatory activity were attributed to CD8+ effector T cells and nature killer cells subsets and a M1-like (high IL1B and TNF, minimal IL6) phenotypic macrophage subcluster. The colander-like lesions were dominant in the bifurcate portion, and the percentage of plasma cells was markedly increased. Immune dysregulation was induced from CD4 naïve T cells, and a downregulation of M2-like macrophage infiltration into the vascular wall. The expression of plasminogen activator, urokinase receptor, urokinase receptor (PLAUR; plasminogen activator) were observed in M2-like (high MRC1 and CD163, virtually no IL1B or TNF) macrophage in bifurcate portion. Notably, one of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) subclusters in the bifurcate portion gained more significantly myofibroblast markers than those in the main portion, and other subclusters remained the function of SMCs. CONCLUSIONS: The regions with colander-like lesions changes had more obviously T cell and macrophages driving immune-inflammatory response and SMCs differentiation, suggesting that combining therapeutic interventions after surgical removal of accessible thrombus may be beneficial. KEY POINTS: This study reveals the comprehensive cellular composition in main/lobar and bifurcate pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA) specimens at the single-cell level. The bifurcate regions with colander had more obviously T cell and macrophages driving immune-inflammatory response and smooth muscle cells (SMCs) differentiation, however, the remodelling of distal or micro-vessels still remained.

title: Introgression Shapes Genetic Variation Associated With Humid Environments in Aedes aegypti Mosquitoes From Saudi Arabia.
abstract: Introgression between genetically distinct populations generates variation that may promote adaptation to diverse environmental conditions. In the mosquito Aedes aegypti, the forest-associated subspecies Aedes aegypti formosus (Aaf) underwent a domestication process approximately 5000 years ago, giving rise to the globally invasive, human-associated arbovirus vector Aedes aegypti aegypti (Aaa). Despite extensive human-mediated transport, the two subspecies remain largely distinct, with admixture documented mainly in coastal Africa and Saudi Arabia. We examined Saudi Arabian Ae. aegypti across climatically contrasting regions - the humid south and arid west- using a Saudi Arabian dataset (11,939 SNPs) to examine within-country genetic and environmental variation and a global dataset (13,455 SNPs) to assess ancestry and admixture in a worldwide context. Genomic analyses revealed strong west-south differentiation, with Jazan Highland showing admixture between subspecies and the highest proportion of Aaf ancestry. Multiple pulses of gene flow into and within southern Saudi Arabia suggest Aaf populations act as a reservoir of genetic variation. Genome-wide scans identified a candidate region associated with the humidity gradient, harbouring an elongase of very long-chain fatty acids (AAEL024147), essential for cuticle production and minimizing water loss. Because the Saudi Arabian genetic background is predominantly the arid-adapted subspecies Aaa, the presence of Aaf ancestry at this locus may reflect localized introgression with adaptive relevance under an increasingly humid environment. Our findings highlight how secondary contact between divergent lineages may contribute to local adaptation in Ae. aegypti, with implications for predicting responses to environmental change.

Despite extensive human-mediated transport, the two subspecies remain largely distinct, with admixture documented mainly in coastal Africa and Saudi Arabia.

title: Improving Apheresis Inlet Flow With a Novel Double-Draw Vascular Access Technique.
abstract: Peripheral intravenous catheters (PIVCs) are the preferred vascular access for apheresis; however, veins that initially appear suitable may develop venous spasms, resulting in poor inlet flow and frequent pressure alarms. Ports used for apheresis can also experience inlet pressure alarms due to catheter or venous occlusion. When conservative measures failed, we implemented a novel double-draw technique in which a second draw line was connected via a four-way stopcock and male-to-male adapter to the initial draw access (either a PIVC or port) to improve inlet flow. The double-draw technique was performed in 26 procedures (therapeutic plasma exchange [TPE], n = 10 and lipoprotein apheresis [LA], n = 16) in 8 patients. During TPE, median negative inlet pressure improved from -179 mmHg (IQR -218 to -69) with single-draw access to -71 mmHg (IQR -78 to -62) following placement of a second draw line (p = 0.0162). Inlet flow rate during TPE improved from median 47 mL/min (IQR, 40-58 mL/min) with single-draw access to 70 mL/min (IQR, 60-75 mL/min) (p = 0.008). During LA, median negative inlet pressure improved from -136 mmHg (IQR -193 to -109) to -59 mmHg (IQR -66 to -47) (p < 0.0001). Median inlet flow rate during LA improved from 70 mL/min (IQR 59-71 mL/min) with single-draw access to median 80 mL/min (IQR 70-80 mL/min) (p = 0.023). Overall 25 of 26 procedures (96.2%) demonstrated an improvement in inlet pressure following implementation of the double-draw technique. All procedures were completed successfully without abandonment of the original access site. The double-draw technique is a novel option for managing inlet pressure alarms during apheresis when conservative measures fail.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Therapeutic Anticoagulation Management in Head and Neck Free Tissue Transfer: A Retrospective Study of 126 Cases.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Existing literature on anticoagulation in head and neck free flap reconstruction largely focuses on postoperative thromboprophylaxis. Less is known about preoperative therapeutic anticoagulation, including how perioperative anticoagulation holds, timing of resumption, and anticoagulant class relate to hemorrhagic, thromboembolic, and flap-related complications. This study evaluates these outcomes in anticoagulated patients undergoing head and neck free flap reconstruction and compares complication rates with matched non-anticoagulated controls. METHODS: A retrospective chart review was performed on patients who underwent free flap reconstruction between 2009 and 2023 and had been on therapeutic anticoagulation for over 1 month preoperatively. A matched control group of non-anticoagulated patients was included for comparison. RESULTS: 126 anticoagulated patients (mean age 71.8 years, 75.4% male) were included. The most common indications for anticoagulation were atrial fibrillation (62.7%) and venous thromboembolism (30.2%). Anticoagulation medications included warfarin (49.2%), apixaban (36.5%), rivaroxaban (12.7%), and dabigatran (1.6%). Anticoagulation was stopped an average of 4.4 days preoperatively and resumed 7.8 days postoperatively. Hemorrhagic complications occurred in 14 patients (11.1%), including hematomas and unrelated bleeding. Thromboembolic complications occurred in 9 patients (7.1%), 6 of which resulted in flap failure. On matched cohort analysis, controls had lower odds of any complication (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21-0.81, p = 0.010), hemorrhagic or thromboembolic complications (OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.11-0.63, p = 0.003), and hemorrhagic complications specifically (OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.09-0.81, p = 0.020), while thromboembolic complication odds were not significantly different between groups (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.15-1.44, p = 0.19). CONCLUSIONS: This study highlights the challenges of managing therapeutic anticoagulation in head and neck free flap surgery, where thromboembolic risk during interruption and hemorrhagic complications upon resumption point to the need for clearer guidelines. Evidence-based protocols are needed to replace discretionary practices and improve outcomes.

This study evaluates these outcomes in anticoagulated patients undergoing head and neck free flap reconstruction and compares complication rates with matched non-anticoagulated controls.

title: Association between admission D-dimer levels and post-stroke epilepsy risk: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-stroke epilepsy (PSE) is a severe complication following acute ischemic stroke (AIS), yet early identification of patients at high risk remains challenging. This study evaluated the association between baseline D-dimer levels and incident PSE within one year after AIS. METHODS: 2 In this secondary analysis of a multicenter retrospective cohort, 21,459 patients with first-ever AIS were included. D-dimer was modeled as a log-transformed continuous variable. Multivariable logistic regression with progressive adjustment, restricted cubic spline analysis, and sensitivity analyses were performed. Internal validation was conducted using bootstrap resampling. RESULTS: The median baseline D-dimer level was 0.92 mg/L (IQR 0.65-1.49). PSE occurred in 936 patients (4.36%). After full adjustment, each doubling of D-dimer was associated with a 3.3-fold increase in PSE odds (OR 3.33, 95% CI 2.94-3.78). The association remained consistent in sensitivity analyses excluding patients with deep vein thrombosis (OR 3.86, 95% CI 3.37-4.43), atrial fibrillation (OR 3.50, 95% CI 3.04-4.04), or extreme D-dimer values (OR 3.41, 95% CI 2.99-3.91). A non-linear relationship was observed, with PSE risk rising more steeply at higher D-dimer levels. The C-statistic for the fully adjusted model was 0.968. CONCLUSION: Elevated baseline D-dimer levels were independently associated with an increased risk of PSE within one year after AIS. As a routinely available biomarker, D-dimer may inform risk assessment in acute stroke units; however, external validation in independent cohorts with prospective PSE ascertainment is required before clinical implementation.

This study evaluated the association between baseline D-dimer levels and incident PSE within one year after AIS. METHODS: 2 In this secondary analysis of a multicenter retrospective cohort, 21,459 patients with first-ever AIS were included.
